reminder: Every [proposition](c:proposition) is either true or false, with no third option.
definition: The law of excluded middle says that $P\lor\neg P$ holds for every [proposition](c:proposition) $P$, so $P$ is true or its [negation](c:negation) is true. [Classical logic](c:classical-logic) accepts this as a rule, and [intuitionistic logic](c:intuitionistic-logic) does not.
examples: In classical logic, every real number $x$ satisfies $x=0$ or $x\neq0$.
Every [decidable proposition](c:decidable-proposition), such as '$n$ is even' for a natural number $n$, satisfies $P\lor\neg P$ even in intuitionistic logic.
Non-example: intuitionistic logic does not prove that every real number $x$ satisfies $x=0$ or $x\neq0$.

steps: Fix one proposition $P$.
In the internal sense, $P$ is [decidable](c:decidable-proposition) when $P\lor\neg P$ holds.
This is the instance of excluded middle at $P$.
Excluded middle asserts this instance for every proposition at the same time.
links.why: It shows that excluded middle is decidability of all propositions at once.

reminder: On a [complex analytic space](c:complex-analytic-space) $X$, the sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\to\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal O_X^\times\to0$ of sheaves is exact.
definition: Let $\mathcal O_X$ be the sheaf of holomorphic functions on a [complex analytic space](c:complex-analytic-space) $X$, and let $\mathcal O_X^\times$ be its sheaf of invertible elements, a [sheaf](c:sheaf) of [abelian groups](c:abelian-group) under multiplication. The exponential exact sequence is $0\to\mathbb Z\to\mathcal O_X\xrightarrow{f\mapsto e^{2\pi if}}\mathcal O_X^\times\to0$, where the first map sends an integer to the constant function. It is an [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) of sheaves, so it is exact on stalks.
examples: On $X=\mathbb C^\times$, the unit $z$ has a holomorphic logarithm near every point, but no single logarithm on all of $\mathbb C^\times$.
Its long exact cohomology sequence contains $H^1(X,\mathcal O_X^\times)\to H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$, which sends a holomorphic line bundle to its [first Chern class](c:first-chern-class).
Non-example: the sequence of global sections $0\to\mathbb Z\to\mathcal O(\mathbb C^\times)\to\mathcal O^\times(\mathbb C^\times)\to0$ is not exact on the right, because $z$ has no logarithm.

reminder: Every density in an exponential family has the form $h(x)\exp(\eta(\theta)\cdot T(x)-A(\theta))$, so the data enter only through $T(x)$.
definition: An exponential family is a family of [probability distributions](c:probability-distribution) $P_\theta$ whose [densities](c:probability-density-function) with respect to a fixed measure have the form $p_\theta(x)=h(x)\exp(\eta(\theta)\cdot T(x)-A(\theta))$. Here $h$ and $T$ do not depend on $\theta$, and $\eta$ and $A$ do not depend on $x$, so all densities have the same support $\{h>0\}$.
examples: The [normal distributions](c:normal-distribution) $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ form an exponential family with $T(x)=(x,x^2)$.
The [Poisson distributions](c:poisson-distribution) with mean $\lambda$ form one, since $p_\lambda(k)=\frac1{k!}\exp(k\log\lambda-\lambda)$.
The [binomial distributions](c:binomial-distribution) with a fixed number of trials $n$ form one, with $T(k)=k$ and $\eta=\log\frac p{1-p}$.
Non-example: the uniform distributions on $[0,\theta]$ do not form one, because the support $[0,\theta]$ depends on $\theta$.

steps: Take the gamma density $f(x)=x^{k-1}e^{-x/\theta}/(\Gamma(k)\theta^k)$ for $x>0$.
Its logarithm is $(k-1)\log x-x/\theta-\log\Gamma(k)-k\log\theta$.
Put $T(x)=(\log x,x)$, $\eta=(k-1,-1/\theta)$ and $h(x)=1$ on $x>0$.
Then the density has the exponential-family form, so the gamma distributions form an exponential family.
links.why: It shows that gamma distributions share the general theory of exponential families.

steps: Expand the exponent of the density $\frac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$ in powers of $x$.
Take $T(x)=(x,x^2)$ and $\eta=(\mu/\sigma^2,-1/(2\sigma^2))$.
Put $h(x)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $A=\mu^2/(2\sigma^2)+\log\sigma$.
The density then has the exponential-family form, so the normal distributions form an exponential family.
links.why: It shows that the normal family is one case of a general pattern.

reminder: The group $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B)$ is the $n$-th cohomology of $\mathrm{Hom}(A,I^\bullet)$ for an injective resolution $I^\bullet$ of $B$.
definition: For [modules](c:module) $A$ and $B$, or objects of an [abelian category](c:abelian-category) with enough injectives, choose an injective resolution $0\to B\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots$. Then $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B)=H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(A,I^\bullet))$, the $n$-th right [derived functor](c:derived-functor) of the [hom-functor](c:hom-functor) $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$, and it does not depend on the resolution. The degree $1$ group classifies extensions $0\to B\to E\to A\to0$.
examples: $\mathrm{Ext}^0(A,B)=\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)$, and $\mathrm{Ext}^n(P,B)=0$ for $n\ge1$ when $P$ is projective.
$\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z/n,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/n$, generated by the extension $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/n\to0$.
$\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$ is in bijection with the equivalence classes of extensions of $A$ by $B$.
Non-example: the functor $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb Z/2,-)$ is not an Ext group, because it is not exact; $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb Z/2,\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/2$ records its failure to be right exact.

steps: Take the functor $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$, which is left exact.
Its right derived functors in degree $n$ are the groups $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,-)$.
In degree $0$, left exactness gives $\mathrm{Ext}^0(A,B)=\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)$.
So the Ext groups extend the Hom functor to a sequence of functors.
links.why: It shows that Ext starts with Hom and adds the higher terms that measure failure of exactness.

reminder: An extension by definitions adds new symbols to a theory, each with an axiom that defines it from the old symbols.
definition: Let $T$ be a [first-order theory](c:first-order-theory) in a language $L$. A theory $T'$ in a larger language is an extension by definitions of $T$ when $T'$ is $T$ plus one defining axiom for each new symbol. For a new relation symbol $R$ the axiom is $R(\bar x)\leftrightarrow\varphi(\bar x)$, and for a new function symbol $f$ it is $f(\bar x)=y\leftrightarrow\varphi(\bar x,y)$ where $T$ proves $\forall\bar x\,\exists!y\,\varphi$, and each $\varphi$ is a [formula](c:formula) of $L$.
examples: In the theory of rings, add a relation $x\mid y$ with the axiom $x\mid y\leftrightarrow\exists z\,(x\cdot z=y)$.
In the theory of groups with only the product symbol, add a constant $e$ with the axiom $\forall x\,(e\cdot x=x)$, because the theory proves that exactly one such element exists.
Non-example: adding a new constant $c$ to the theory of fields with only the axiom $c\neq0$ is not an extension by definitions, because no formula of the old language defines $c$.

steps: Let $T'$ be an extension by definitions of $T$, and replace each new symbol in a formula by its defining formula.
Under this translation, each defining axiom becomes a theorem of $T$, and formulas of the old language stay unchanged.
So a proof in $T'$ of an old formula turns into a proof in $T$ of the same formula.
Hence $T'$ proves no new statement of $L$, and it is a [conservative extension](c:conservative-extension) of $T$.
links.why: It shows that adding defined symbols never changes what the old language can prove.

reminder: An extra degeneracy is a family of maps $s_{-1},s_0,s_1,\dots$ that go up one level and split an augmented simplicial object.
definition: Let $X_\bullet\to X_{-1}$ be an augmented [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) with augmentation $\epsilon:X_0\to X_{-1}$. An extra degeneracy consists of maps $s_{-1}:X_{-1}\to X_0$ and $s_n:X_n\to X_{n+1}$ for $n\ge0$ with $\epsilon s_{-1}=\mathrm{id}$, $d_0s_n=\mathrm{id}$ and $d_1s_0=s_{-1}\epsilon$. They also obey the [simplicial identities](c:simplicial-identities) with an index shift: $d_{i+1}s_{n+1}=s_nd_i$ and $\sigma_{i+1}s_n=s_{n+1}\sigma_i$, so $s_{-1}$ is a [section](c:section) of $\epsilon$.
examples: The standard simplex $\Delta[n]$ augmented over a point has an extra degeneracy: $s_{-1}$ picks the vertex $0$, and $s_k$ puts the vertex $0$ in front of a simplex.
The augmented [Čech nerve](c:cech-nerve) of a morphism $f:Y\to Z$ with a section has an extra degeneracy built from that section.

Non-example: in topological spaces, the augmented Čech nerve of $\mathbb R\to S^1$, $t\mapsto e^{2\pi it}$, has no extra degeneracy, because $s_{-1}$ would be a continuous section of this map and none exists.

reminder: The number $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)$ is the largest number of edges in an $n$-vertex [graph](c:graph) that has no copy of $H$.
definition: For a [graph](c:graph) $H$ and an integer $n\ge1$, the extremal number $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)$ is the maximum number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices with no [subgraph](c:is-subgraph) isomorphic to $H$. A graph that reaches this maximum is an extremal graph for $H$.
examples: $\mathrm{ex}(n,K_3)=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ (Mantel), reached by the complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ and $\lceil n/2\rceil$.
$\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{r+1})$ is the number of edges of the [Turán graph](c:turan-graph) on $n$ vertices with $r$ parts (Turán).
$\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{1,2})=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, because forbidding a path with two edges leaves only a matching.
Non-example: a path with $n-1$ edges has no triangle, but $n-1<\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ for $n\ge4$, so $n-1$ is not $\mathrm{ex}(n,K_3)$.

reminder: An f-divergence measures how far $P$ is from $Q$ by averaging $f(dP/dQ)$ for a convex $f$ with $f(1)=0$.
definition: Let $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be a [convex function](c:convex-function) with $f(1)=0$, and let $P\ll Q$ be [probability measures](c:probability-measure). The f-divergence is $D_f(P\|Q)=\int f\!\left(\frac{dP}{dQ}\right)dQ$, where $dP/dQ$ is the [Radon–Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative). By Jensen's inequality, $D_f(P\|Q)\ge0$, with equality when $P=Q$.
examples: The choice $f(t)=t\log t$ gives the [Kullback–Leibler divergence](c:kullback-leibler-divergence).
The choice $f(t)=\frac12|t-1|$ gives the [total variation distance](c:total-variation-distance).
The choice $f(t)=(t-1)^2$ gives the chi-squared divergence $\int(dP/dQ-1)^2\,dQ$.
Non-example: the Wasserstein distance is not an f-divergence, because it depends on distances between points of the sample space, while $D_f$ depends only on the ratio $dP/dQ$.

steps: Choose $f(t)=t\log t$, a convex function with $f(1)=0$.
Then the f-divergence equals $\int\frac{dP}{dQ}\log\frac{dP}{dQ}\,dQ$.
Since $\frac{dP}{dQ}\,dQ=dP$, this equals $\int\log\frac{dP}{dQ}\,dP$.
That is the [Kullback–Leibler divergence](c:kullback-leibler-divergence) of $P$ from $Q$.
links.why: It shows that the Kullback–Leibler divergence is one member of the f-divergence family.

steps: Choose $f(t)=\frac12|t-1|$, a convex function with $f(1)=0$.
Then the f-divergence equals $\frac12\int\left|\frac{dP}{dQ}-1\right|dQ$.
This equals $\frac12\int|dP-dQ|$, which is the [total variation distance](c:total-variation-distance) of $P$ and $Q$.
links.why: It shows that the total variation distance is also an f-divergence.

reminder: A factorization writes an element as a product of other elements, usually of a special kind such as primes.
definition: A factorization of an element $a$ of a [monoid](c:monoid), such as the integers under multiplication or a [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring), is an expression $a=a_1a_2\cdots a_n$ as a product of other elements. One usually asks that each factor is of a special kind, such as a [prime number](c:prime-number) or an irreducible polynomial. In linear algebra and analysis, the word also means a product of matrices or functions with prescribed properties.
examples: $60=2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot5$ is a factorization of the integer $60$ into primes.
$x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ is a factorization of a polynomial into polynomials of degree $1$.
A square matrix $A$ with all leading minors nonzero factors as $A=LU$, with $L$ unit lower triangular and $U$ upper triangular.
Non-example: $x^2+1$ has no factorization into two polynomials of degree $1$ with real coefficients.

steps: Take an integer $n\ge2$ and a factorization $n=a_1\cdots a_k$ into integers $a_i\ge2$.
Ask that each factor $a_i$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number).
The result is the [prime factorization](c:prime-factorization) of $n$, which is unique up to the order of the factors.
links.why: It shows what the special requirement on the factors adds, and why the result is unique.

reminder: A representation is faithful when only the neutral element of the group acts as the identity.
definition: A [representation](c:group-representation) $\rho:G\to GL(V)$ of a [group](c:group) $G$ on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is faithful when $\rho$ is an [injective map](c:injective-map), that is, $\rho(g)=\rho(h)$ implies $g=h$. Equivalently, the kernel of $\rho$ is trivial, so $G$ is isomorphic to the group of matrices $\rho(G)$.
examples: The permutation representation of $S_n$ on $\mathbb C^n$ is faithful, because every non-identity permutation moves a basis vector.
The inclusion $SO(n)\hookrightarrow GL_n(\mathbb R)$ is a faithful representation.
The map $k\mapsto e^{2\pi ik/n}$ gives a faithful representation of $\mathbb Z/n$ on $\mathbb C$.
Non-example: the sign representation of $S_n$ for $n\ge3$ is not faithful, because every even permutation acts as $1$.

steps: A linear representation $\rho$ of $G$ on $V$ gives an action $g\cdot v=\rho(g)v$ of $G$ on the set $V$.
This action is effective when only the neutral element fixes every vector.
That condition says $\rho(g)=\mathrm{id}$ only for $g=e$, so the representation is faithful.
links.why: It shows that a faithful representation is an effective action by linear maps.

steps: View the group $G$ as a one-object category whose morphisms are the elements of $G$.
A representation $\rho$ is a functor from this category to vector spaces, which sends the object to $V$.
On morphisms, the functor is the map $g\mapsto\rho(g)$.
The representation is faithful exactly when this map is injective, which is the definition of a [faithful functor](c:faithful).
links.why: It shows that faithful representations are faithful functors, so categorical results apply.

reminder: The Fatou set of $f$ is the set of points that have a neighbourhood where the iterates of $f$ form a [normal family](c:normal-family).
definition: Let $f$ be a [rational function](c:rational-function) of degree at least $2$, viewed as a map of the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere). A point $z$ is in the Fatou set of $f$ when it has an open neighbourhood $U$ such that the iterates $f^{\circ n}|_U$ form a [normal family](c:normal-family). The complement of the Fatou set is the [Julia set](c:julia-set).
examples: For $f(z)=z^2$, the Fatou set is $\{|z|<1\}\cup\{|z|>1\}\cup\{\infty\}$, and the Julia set is the unit circle.
For $f(z)=z^2-2$, the Julia set is the segment $[-2,2]$, and the Fatou set is its complement.
The basin of attraction of every attracting fixed point lies in the Fatou set.
Non-example: a point on the unit circle is not in the Fatou set of $z^2$, because the iterates $z^{2^n}$ are not equicontinuous on any neighbourhood of it.

reminder: A feedback control sets the input of a system from its current state or output, so that the input reacts to the system.
definition: For a control system $\dot x=f(x,u)$, a feedback control is a rule $u=k(x)$, or $u=k(y)$ for an output $y=h(x)$, that gives the input $u$ as a function of what the system shows now. The closed-loop system $\dot x=f(x,k(x))$ is an [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) without input, and one often asks that its zero solution is [Lyapunov stable](c:lyapunov-stability).
examples: For $\dot x=x+u$, the feedback $u=-2x$ gives the closed loop $\dot x=-x$, which is stable.
A thermostat switches a heater on or off from the measured room temperature.
A cruise control changes the throttle from the difference between the measured speed and the wanted speed.
Non-example: a heater that follows a fixed timer $u(t)$ ignores the room temperature, so it is open-loop control and not feedback.

reminder: A feedback vertex set is a set of vertices whose removal leaves a graph with no cycle.
definition: A feedback vertex set of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ is a set $S$ of [vertices](c:vertex) such that deleting $S$, with its incident edges, leaves an [acyclic graph](c:acyclic-graph). Equivalently, every [cycle](c:cycle) of $G$ contains a vertex of $S$.
examples: In the cycle graph $C_n$, any single vertex is a feedback vertex set.
In the complete graph $K_n$ with $n\ge2$, every set of $n-2$ vertices is a minimum feedback vertex set, because any three remaining vertices form a triangle.
In a tree, the empty set is a feedback vertex set.
Non-example: in two disjoint triangles, one vertex is not enough, because the other triangle stays.

reminder: The Feynman propagator is the [fundamental solution](c:fundamental-solution) of $\Box+m^2$ that moves positive frequencies forward in time and negative frequencies backward.
definition: On a [globally hyperbolic spacetime](c:globally-hyperbolic-spacetime), a Feynman propagator is a [fundamental solution](c:fundamental-solution) $G_F$ of the [Klein-Gordon equation](c:klein-gordon-equation), so $(\Box+m^2)G_F=\delta$ up to a constant that conventions fix. Its singularities obey the Feynman condition: positive-frequency parts propagate forward in time, and negative-frequency parts propagate backward. In Minkowski spacetime, $G_F(x,y)$ is the vacuum expectation of the [time-ordered product](c:time-ordered-product) $T\phi(x)\phi(y)$ of the [free field](c:free-field) $\phi$, up to the same constant.
examples: In Minkowski spacetime, $G_F(x-y)=\int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}\frac{i\,e^{-ip\cdot(x-y)}}{p^2-m^2+i\epsilon}$, with the $+i\epsilon$ prescription.
Each internal line of a Feynman diagram of a scalar field theory stands for one Feynman propagator.
Non-example: the retarded propagator also solves $(\Box+m^2)G=\delta$, but it vanishes outside the future light cone, so it is not the Feynman propagator.

steps: Take the Klein-Gordon operator $P=\Box+m^2$.
A [fundamental solution](c:fundamental-solution) of $P$ is a distribution $G$ with $PG=\delta$.
The Feynman propagator satisfies this equation, so it is a fundamental solution.
It adds the Feynman boundary condition, which selects one fundamental solution among many.
links.why: It shows that the Feynman propagator is one chosen Green function, not the only one.

reminder: A filtered colimit is a [colimit](c:colimit) over an index category in which every finite diagram has a cocone.
definition: A category $J$ is [filtered](c:filtered-category) when it is nonempty, any two objects have morphisms to a common object, and any two parallel morphisms are equalized by a later morphism. A filtered colimit is the [colimit](c:colimit) of a diagram $D:J\to\mathcal C$ with $J$ filtered. In sets, it is the disjoint union of all $D_j$ in which $x\in D_j$ and $y\in D_k$ are equal when they have the same image in some $D_l$.
examples: The union of a chain of subsets $A_0\subseteq A_1\subseteq\cdots$ is the filtered colimit of the inclusions.
$\mathbb Z[1/p]$ is the filtered colimit of $\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{p}\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{p}\mathbb Z\to\cdots$.
The [stalk](c:stalk) $\mathcal F_x$ of a sheaf is the filtered colimit of $\mathcal F(U)$ over the open neighbourhoods $U$ of $x$.
Non-example: the coproduct $A\sqcup B$ is a colimit over a discrete category with two objects, which is not filtered, because $A$ and $B$ have no common upper bound.

steps: A filtered colimit is the colimit of a diagram $D:J\to\mathcal C$ in a category $\mathcal C$.
So the cocone and the universal property of a [colimit](c:colimit) apply without change.
The special case adds one condition: the index category $J$ is filtered.
links.why: It shows that every fact about colimits holds, and that filteredness is the extra condition.

steps: Let $(I,\le)$ be a directed set: it is nonempty, and any two elements have an upper bound.
View $I$ as a category with one morphism $i\to j$ when $i\le j$.
Any two objects map to a common object, and parallel morphisms are equal, so this category is filtered.
Hence every [directed colimit](c:directed-colimit) is a filtered colimit.
links.why: It shows that filtered colimits include directed colimits and sequential colimits as simple cases.

reminder: A filtered probability space is a probability space with an increasing family of sub-sigma-algebras that records the information known at each time.
definition: A filtered probability space is a quadruple $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in T},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ is a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) and $P$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) on $\mathcal F$. The index set $T$ is ordered, often $\mathbb N$ or $[0,\infty)$, and $(\mathcal F_t)$ is a [filtration](c:filtration): each $\mathcal F_t$ is a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) with $\mathcal F_s\subseteq\mathcal F_t\subseteq\mathcal F$ whenever $s\le t$.
examples: For independent coin tosses $X_1,X_2,\dots$, put $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ to get a filtered probability space.
For a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_t)$, the natural filtration $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(X_s:s\le t)$ makes the underlying space a filtered probability space.
Non-example: for independent coin tosses $X_1,X_2$, the family $\mathcal F_1=\sigma(X_1)$, $\mathcal F_2=\sigma(X_2)$ is not a filtration, because $\mathcal F_1\not\subseteq\mathcal F_2$.

steps: Take a filtered probability space and forget the filtration.
The triple $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a [measure space](c:measure-space), because $P$ is a measure on $\mathcal F$.
The special case adds that $P(\Omega)=1$ and that a filtration is given.
links.why: It shows that results about measure spaces apply to the underlying space of a filtered probability space.

reminder: The finite difference method replaces derivatives by difference quotients of grid values, which turns a differential equation into algebraic equations.
definition: The finite difference method approximates a solution $u$ of a [differential equation](c:differential-equation) by values $u_i\approx u(x_i)$ on a grid with step $h$. It replaces each [derivative](c:derivative) by a [difference quotient](c:difference-quotient) of nearby grid values, for example $u'(x_i)\approx(u_{i+1}-u_i)/h$ and $u''(x_i)\approx(u_{i+1}-2u_i+u_{i-1})/h^2$, and then solves the resulting algebraic equations.
examples: For $-u''=f$ on $[0,1]$ with $u(0)=u(1)=0$, central differences give the tridiagonal system $-u_{i-1}+2u_i-u_{i+1}=h^2f(x_i)$.
The forward Euler method $u_{n+1}=u_n+h\,g(t_n,u_n)$ for $u'=g(t,u)$ is a finite difference method.
The upwind scheme $u_i^{n+1}=u_i^n-a\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x}(u_i^n-u_{i-1}^n)$ for $u_t+au_x=0$ with $a>0$ is a finite difference method.
Non-example: the finite element method uses a weak form and piecewise polynomial basis functions, not difference quotients of grid values, so it is not a finite difference method.

reminder: A finite-dimensional distribution is the joint law of the values of a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) at finitely many times.
definition: Let $(X_t)_{t\in T}$ be a real-valued [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process). For a finite set of times $t_1,\dots,t_n\in T$, the finite-dimensional distribution $\mu_{t_1\dots t_n}$ is the [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution) of $(X_{t_1},\dots,X_{t_n})$, a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) on $\mathbb R^n$. The family of all of them is consistent: permuting the times permutes the coordinates, and deleting a time gives a marginal.
examples: For Brownian motion $B$ and times $t_1<\dots<t_n$, the vector $(B_{t_1},\dots,B_{t_n})$ is centered Gaussian with covariance $\min(t_i,t_j)$.
For independent identically distributed variables with law $\mu$, the law of $(X_{k_1},\dots,X_{k_n})$ is the product measure $\mu^{\otimes n}$.
Non-example: the law of $\sup_{t\le1}B_t$ is not a finite-dimensional distribution, because the supremum depends on the values at infinitely many times.

reminder: A finite spectrum is a [CW-spectrum](c:cw-spectrum) with only finitely many cells.
definition: A finite spectrum is a [CW-spectrum](c:cw-spectrum) that is built from finitely many cells. Equivalently, up to homotopy equivalence, it has the form $\Sigma^{-n}\Sigma^\infty X$ for a [finite CW complex](c:finite-cw-complex) $X$ and an integer $n$.
examples: The [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum) $\mathbb S$ has one cell, so it is finite.
The [suspension spectrum](c:suspension-spectrum) $\Sigma^\infty X$ of a finite CW complex $X$ is a finite spectrum.
The Moore spectrum $\mathbb S/n$, the cofibre of $n:\mathbb S\to\mathbb S$, has two cells.
Non-example: the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum $H\mathbb Z$ is not finite, because its mod $2$ homology is infinite in total, while a finite spectrum has finite total homology.

steps: Take a finite spectrum $E$ and choose a cell structure on it with finitely many cells.
With this structure, $E$ is a [CW-spectrum](c:cw-spectrum).
The finite case adds that the number of cells is finite.
links.why: It shows that finite spectra are exactly the CW-spectra with a finite cell count.

reminder: The finite volume method updates the average of a conserved quantity in each cell by the net flux through the cell faces.
definition: For a [conservation law](c:conservation-law) $u_t+\nabla\cdot F(u)=0$, the finite volume method divides the domain into cells $C_i$ and tracks the cell averages $\bar u_i$. It integrates the law over each cell, writes the boundary term as a sum of numerical fluxes through the faces, and updates $\bar u_i$ by the net flux. This keeps the total amount of the conserved quantity exact, up to the flux through the domain boundary.
examples: In one dimension the update is $\bar u_i^{n+1}=\bar u_i^n-\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x}(F_{i+1/2}-F_{i-1/2})$, where $F_{i\pm1/2}$ are numerical fluxes.
The upwind scheme for $u_t+au_x=0$ with $a>0$ is a finite volume method with $F_{i+1/2}=a\bar u_i$.
The Lax-Wendroff scheme for a scalar conservation law can be written in this flux form.
Non-example: for Burgers' equation $u_t+(u^2/2)_x=0$, the scheme $u_i^{n+1}=u_i^n-\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x}u_i^n(u_i^n-u_{i-1}^n)$ is not in flux form, and it can give shocks with the wrong speed.

reminder: A module is finitely presented when it has finitely many generators and finitely many relations among them.
definition: A [module](c:module) $M$ over a ring $R$ is finitely presented when there is an [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $R^q\to R^p\to M\to0$ with $p$ and $q$ [natural numbers](c:natural-number). Equivalently, $M$ has $p$ generators, and the relations among them are generated by $q$ elements.
examples: The free module $R^n$ is finitely presented.
For an ideal $I$ with finitely many generators, $R/I$ is finitely presented; for example $\mathbb Z/n$.
Over a [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring), every finitely generated module is finitely presented.
Non-example: for $R=k[x_1,x_2,\dots]$, the module $R/(x_1,x_2,\dots)\cong k$ has one generator but is not finitely presented, because the ideal $(x_1,x_2,\dots)$ is not finitely generated.

steps: Let $R^q\to R^p\xrightarrow{\pi}M\to0$ be a presentation of $M$.
Exactness at $M$ says that $\pi$ is surjective.
So the images of the $p$ standard basis vectors generate $M$, and $M$ is [finitely generated](c:finitely-generated-module).
The finitely presented case adds that the kernel of $\pi$, the module of relations, is generated by $q$ elements.
links.why: It shows that finite presentation is finite generation plus finitely many relations.

steps: Let $M$ be a [coherent module](c:coherent-module): it is finitely generated, and each finitely generated submodule is finitely presented.
The module $M$ is a finitely generated submodule of itself.
So $M$ is finitely presented.
Coherence adds the condition on all finitely generated submodules.
links.why: It shows that every coherent module is finitely presented, and that coherence is a stronger condition.

reminder: The first Chern class $c_1(L)\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ of a complex [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L$ classifies $L$ up to isomorphism.
definition: For a complex [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L$ on a nice space $X$ with classifying map $f:X\to\mathbb{CP}^\infty$, the first Chern class is $c_1(L)=f^*(x)\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$, where $x$ is a fixed generator of the [cohomology](c:cohomology) group $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)$ of infinite [complex projective space](c:complex-projective-space). It satisfies $c_1(L\otimes L')=c_1(L)+c_1(L')$. For a complex [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E$, one sets $c_1(E)=c_1(\det E)$, where $\det E$ is the [determinant line bundle](c:determinant-line-bundle).
examples: The trivial line bundle has $c_1=0$.

On $\mathbb{CP}^1$, the [tautological line bundle](c:tautological-line-bundle) has $c_1=-1$ and its dual $\mathcal O(1)$ has $c_1=1$, for the standard generator of $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^1;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$.
The tangent bundle of $\mathbb{CP}^1$ has $c_1=2$, which equals the Euler characteristic of the sphere.
Non-example: the Möbius bundle over $S^1$ is a real line bundle, so it has no Chern class; its invariant is the [Stiefel-Whitney class](c:stiefel-whitney-class) $w_1\in H^1(S^1;\mathbb Z/2)$.

steps: The total [Chern class](c:chern-class) of a complex vector bundle $E$ is $c(E)=1+c_1(E)+c_2(E)+\cdots$.
Its component in degree $2$ is the first Chern class $c_1(E)\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$.
For a line bundle $L$ all higher terms vanish, so $c(L)=1+c_1(L)$.
links.why: It shows that the first Chern class is the degree-two piece of the full Chern class, and the only piece for line bundles.

steps: A [characteristic class](c:characteristic-class) assigns to each bundle $E\to X$ a cohomology class of $X$, natural under pullback.
The first Chern class assigns $c_1(E)\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ to each complex vector bundle.
It is natural: $c_1(g^*E)=g^*c_1(E)$ for every map $g:Y\to X$.
links.why: It shows that the first Chern class is a characteristic class, so the general theory of such classes applies.

reminder: A flag is a chain of nested objects $V_0\subset V_1\subset\cdots\subset V_k$, such as subspaces of a vector space.
definition: A flag in a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is a chain of [linear subspaces](c:linear-subspace) $0=V_0\subsetneq V_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq V_k=V$, and it is complete when $\dim V_i=i$ for all $i$. In any [partial order](c:partial-order), a flag is a maximal totally ordered subset.
examples: In $\mathbb R^3$, the chain $0\subset\langle e_1\rangle\subset\langle e_1,e_2\rangle\subset\mathbb R^3$ of a line in a plane is a complete flag.
A flag of a $3$-dimensional polytope is a chain vertex $\subset$ edge $\subset$ facet of faces that contain each other.
In the divisors of $12$ ordered by divisibility, the chain $1\mid2\mid4\mid12$ is a flag.
Non-example: two different lines $L_1,L_2$ in $\mathbb R^3$ do not form a flag, because neither line contains the other.

reminder: The flag bundle of a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E\to X$ has as fibre over $x$ the space of complete flags in $E_x$.
definition: Let $E\to X$ be a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) of rank $n$. Its flag bundle $\mathrm{Fl}(E)\to X$ is the [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle) whose fibre over a point $x\in X$ is the [flag variety](c:flag-variety) of complete [flags](c:flag) $0=V_0\subset V_1\subset\cdots\subset V_n=E_x$.
examples: For $X$ a point, $\mathrm{Fl}(E)$ is the complete flag variety $GL_n(\mathbb C)/B$ of $\mathbb C^n$.
For a rank $2$ bundle, $\mathrm{Fl}(E)$ is the [projective bundle](c:projective-bundle) $\mathbb P(E)$, because a complete flag in a plane is a line.
The pullback of $E$ to $\mathrm{Fl}(E)$ has a filtration with line bundle quotients, which gives the splitting principle.
Non-example: for a rank $3$ bundle, the projective bundle $\mathbb P(E)$ has fibres $\mathbb P^2$ that record one line only, so it is not the flag bundle.

reminder: Floer homology is Morse homology for a functional on an infinite-dimensional space, with flow lines given by solutions of an elliptic equation.
definition: Floer homology is the common name of several homology theories built like [Morse homology](c:morse-homology), but for a functional such as an [action functional](c:action-functional) on an infinite-dimensional space. The chain complex has the critical points of the functional as generators, and its differential counts isolated solutions of an [elliptic](c:elliptic-operator) equation that join two critical points, where the linearized operator is a [Fredholm operator](c:fredholm-operator). In Hamiltonian Floer homology of a closed [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold), the generators are the periodic orbits of a Hamiltonian.
examples: Hamiltonian Floer homology of a closed symplectic manifold $M$ is isomorphic to the homology of $M$ with suitable coefficients, which gives lower bounds for the number of periodic orbits (Arnold conjecture).
Instanton Floer homology of a homology $3$-sphere uses the Chern-Simons functional on connections, and its differential counts Yang-Mills instantons on the cylinder.

Non-example: Morse homology of a [Morse function](c:morse-function) on a closed finite-dimensional manifold is not Floer homology, because its flow lines solve an ordinary differential equation and not an elliptic equation.

steps: Take a [Morse function](c:morse-function) $f$ on a closed symplectic manifold, and its Morse complex of critical points and gradient flow lines.
Choose the time-independent Hamiltonian $H=\varepsilon f$ with $\varepsilon$ small, so that the periodic orbits of $H$ are the constant loops at critical points of $f$.
For such a small Hamiltonian, the Floer trajectories between these loops are the gradient flow lines of $f$.
So the Floer complex equals the Morse complex, and Floer homology extends Morse homology to infinite-dimensional problems.
links.why: It shows that Floer homology reduces to Morse homology in the simplest case, and so explains its counting rules.

reminder: A flow is a continuous action $\phi$ of a time monoid on a space, with $\phi_0=\mathrm{id}$ and $\phi_{s+t}=\phi_s\circ\phi_t$.
definition: A flow of a [topological monoid](c:topological-monoid) $(\tau,+)$ on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $\alpha$ is a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $\phi:\tau\times\alpha\to\alpha$ with $\phi(0,x)=x$ and $\phi(s+t,x)=\phi(s,\phi(t,x))$ for all $s,t\in\tau$ and $x\in\alpha$. Usually $\tau=\mathbb R$ or $\tau=\mathbb N$, and one writes $\phi_t=\phi(t,\cdot)$.
examples: The translation $\phi_t(x)=x+t$ is a flow on $\mathbb R$.
For a matrix $A$, the maps $\phi_t(x)=e^{tA}x$ form a flow on $\mathbb R^n$ that solves $\dot x=Ax$.
The rotations $\phi_t(z)=e^{it}z$ form a flow on the unit circle.
Non-example: $\phi_t(x)=x+t^2$ is not a flow, because $\phi_{s+t}(x)=x+s^2+2st+t^2$ differs from $\phi_s(\phi_t(x))=x+s^2+t^2$.

steps: Let $\phi:\tau\times\alpha\to\alpha$ be a flow, and view $(\tau,+)$ as an additive semigroup.
The rule $\phi(s+t,x)=\phi(s,\phi(t,x))$ says that $\phi$ is an [additive semigroup action](c:add-semigroup-action) on the set $\alpha$.
The flow adds that $\phi(0,x)=x$ and that $\phi$ is continuous on $\tau\times\alpha$.
links.why: It shows that a flow is an ordinary action plus the identity law and continuity.

reminder: The flow map of a [vector field](c:vector-field) sends each point to its position after time $t$ along the solution curve.
definition: Let $v$ be a time-dependent [vector field](c:vector-field) on a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ that is Lipschitz in space. The flow map $\varphi_t$ sends a point $X$ to $\varphi_t(X)=y(t)$, where $y$ solves the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $\dot y=v(y,t)$ with $y(0)=X$. In continuum mechanics, $X$ labels a material point and $\varphi_t(X)$ is its position at time $t$.
examples: For $v(x)=Ax$ with a constant matrix $A$, the flow map is $\varphi_t(x)=e^{tA}x$.
For the rotation field $v(x,y)=(-y,x)$, the flow map $\varphi_t$ is the rotation by the angle $t$.
For the stretching field $v(x)=\lambda x$ on $\mathbb R^n$, $\varphi_t(x)=e^{\lambda t}x$ multiplies volumes by $e^{n\lambda t}$.
Non-example: the velocity field $v$ is not the flow map; for $v(x)=Ax$ the flow map is $e^{tA}x$ and not $Ax$.

reminder: A foliation splits a manifold into disjoint connected submanifolds, the leaves, that locally look like parallel slices of $\mathbb R^n$.
definition: A foliation of dimension $p$ of a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M^n$ is a partition of $M$ into connected [immersed](c:immersion) [submanifolds](c:submanifold) of dimension $p$, the leaves. Every point has a chart $U\to\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^{n-p}$ in which the connected pieces of the leaves in $U$ are exactly the slices $\mathbb R^p\times\{c\}$.
examples: The horizontal lines $\mathbb R\times\{c\}$ foliate $\mathbb R^2$.
The Kronecker foliation of the torus $T^2$ by lines of irrational slope has leaves that are lines, and each leaf is dense.
The connected components of the fibres of a [submersion](c:submersion) $M\to N$ form a foliation of $M$.
Non-example: the concentric circles about $0$ do not foliate $\mathbb R^2$, because the leaf $\{0\}$ has dimension $0$ while the other leaves have dimension $1$.

steps: Let $f:M\to N$ be a [submersion](c:submersion), so $df$ is onto at every point.
By the local normal form of submersions, each point has a chart in which $f$ is the projection $(x,y)\mapsto y$.
In that chart, the fibres of $f$ are the slices $y=c$.
So the connected components of the fibres are the leaves of a foliation, which keeps this local form but needs no global map $f$.
links.why: It shows that a foliation is locally the fibration of a submersion, though globally it need not come from one.

reminder: Forcing adjoins a generic object to a model of set theory, to make chosen statements true or false in the new model.
definition: Let $M$ be a countable transitive [model](c:model) of [ZFC](c:zfc) and let $\mathbb P$ be a [partial order](c:partial-order) in $M$ with a largest element. A filter $G\subseteq\mathbb P$ is $M$-generic when it meets every dense subset of $\mathbb P$ that belongs to $M$. The forcing extension $M[G]$ is the smallest transitive model of ZFC that contains $M$ and $G$ and has the same ordinals, and $p\Vdash\varphi$ says that $\varphi$ holds in $M[G]$ for every generic $G$ with $p\in G$.
examples: Cohen forcing, with finite partial functions $\omega\to2$ ordered by extension, adds a new real number.
Adding $\aleph_2$ Cohen reals to a model of ZFC with the generalized continuum hypothesis gives a model where the continuum hypothesis fails.
The collapse forcing for $\kappa$ makes the cardinal $\kappa$ countable in $M[G]$.
Non-example: passing from the universe to the [constructible universe](c:constructible-universe) $L$ is not forcing, because $L$ is a smaller inner model, while a forcing extension is larger.

reminder: A formula is a finite string of symbols that is built from atomic formulas with connectives and quantifiers, following the grammar of a language.
definition: In [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic) with a language $L$, the atomic formulas are $t_1=t_2$ and $R(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ for terms $t_i$ of $L$. If $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are formulas, then so are $\neg\varphi$, $\varphi\wedge\psi$, $\varphi\vee\psi$ and $\varphi\to\psi$, and so are $\forall x\,\varphi$ and $\exists x\,\varphi$, built with the [universal quantifier](c:universal-quantifier) and the [existential quantifier](c:existential-quantifier). A [variable](c:variable) of a formula that no quantifier binds is a free variable.
examples: In the language $\{<\}$ of orders, $\forall x\,\exists y\,(x<y)$ is a formula.
In the language of rings, $x+0=x$ is an atomic formula with the free variable $x$.
Non-example: $\exists f\,\forall x\,(f(x)=x)$ is not a first-order formula, because it quantifies over a function $f$ and not over elements.

steps: Start with a formula $\varphi$ of a first-order language.
Add the condition that $\varphi$ has no free [variable](c:variable).
Then a quantifier binds every variable of $\varphi$, so $\varphi$ is a [sentence](c:sentence).
A sentence is true or false in each structure, while a general formula also needs values for its free variables.
links.why: It shows what a sentence adds to a formula: no free variables, so a truth value in every structure.

reminder: A framed link is a [link](c:link) in which each component carries a framing, a nowhere-zero normal vector field.
definition: A framed link in a $3$-manifold $M$ is a [link](c:link) $L\subset M$ together with a framing of each component: a choice of nowhere-zero field in the [normal bundle](c:normal-bundle) of the component, or equivalently an embedding of a [solid torus](c:solid-torus) with the component as its core. In the $3$-sphere, the framing of a component is determined, up to homotopy, by an integer: the linking number of the component with its push-off along the field.
examples: The [unknot](c:unknot) with framing $n$ is the boundary curve of a ribbon with $n$ full twists.
Every [link diagram](c:link-diagram) gives a framed link by the blackboard framing, which pushes each component off along the plane of the diagram.
The Hopf link with framings $a$ and $b$ has linking matrix with $a$ and $b$ on the diagonal and $\pm1$ off the diagonal.
Non-example: a link drawn as plain embedded circles, with no chosen normal field, is not a framed link until each component receives a framing.

steps: Take a framed link and forget the framing of every component.
What remains is a set of disjoint embedded circles, which is a [link](c:link).
The framed case adds one choice for each component, a framing, which in the $3$-sphere is an integer.
links.why: It shows that a framed link is a link with one extra integer of data per component in the $3$-sphere.

reminder: A framed manifold is a manifold with a chosen trivialization of its tangent bundle, that is, one global frame.
definition: A framing of a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ of dimension $n$ is an isomorphism $TM\cong M\times\mathbb R^n$ of its [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle), equivalently a [section](c:section) of its [frame bundle](c:frame-bundle). A framed manifold is a manifold together with a framing.
examples: Every [Lie group](c:lie-group) is framed by a basis of left-invariant vector fields.
The spheres $S^1$, $S^3$ and $S^7$ have framings.
Every open subset of $\mathbb R^n$ has the framing by the coordinate vector fields.
Non-example: $S^2$ has no framing, because a framing would give a nowhere-zero vector field, and the hairy ball theorem forbids that.

steps: Take a framed manifold and forget the framing.
What remains is a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ with its tangent bundle.
The framed case adds a global trivialization $TM\cong M\times\mathbb R^n$, which exists only when $M$ is parallelizable.
links.why: It shows that framing is extra structure that only some manifolds admit.

reminder: A Fréchet space is a complete metrizable [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space), given by countably many seminorms.
definition: A Fréchet space is a [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space) whose topology is [metrizable](c:metrizable-space) and [complete](c:complete-topological-vector-space). Equivalently, it is a vector space with a countable family of [seminorms](c:seminorm) $p_1\le p_2\le\cdots$ that separates points, which is complete for the metric $d(x,y)=\sum_n2^{-n}\min(1,p_n(x-y))$.
examples: Every [Banach space](c:banach-space) is a Fréchet space, and so is $\mathbb R^n$.
The space $C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with the seminorms $p_n(f)=\max_{k\le n}\sup_{|x|\le n}|f^{(k)}(x)|$ is a Fréchet space that has no norm.
The Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ is a Fréchet space.
Non-example: the space $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ of test functions with its inductive limit topology is not metrizable, so it is not a Fréchet space.

steps: Let $X$ be a [Banach space](c:banach-space) with norm $\|\cdot\|$.
The single [seminorm](c:seminorm) $p_1=\|\cdot\|$ is a countable family that separates points.
The metric it induces is complete, so $X$ is complete, metrizable and locally convex.
Hence $X$ is a Fréchet space, and Fréchet spaces allow countably many seminorms in place of one norm.
links.why: It shows that every Banach space is a Fréchet space and what the Fréchet notion adds.

steps: Let $X$ be a Fréchet space with seminorms $p_n$.
The seminorms generate the topology, so $0$ has a base of convex neighbourhoods and $X$ is a [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space).
The Fréchet case adds that the family is countable, so the topology is metrizable, and that $X$ is complete.
links.why: It shows which two conditions a Fréchet space adds to local convexity.

reminder: An action of a group is free when $g\cdot x=x$ for some point $x$ forces $g=e$.
definition: An [action](c:group-action) of a [group](c:group) $G$ on a set $X$ is free when $g\cdot x=x$ implies $g=e$, for all $g\in G$ and $x\in X$. Equivalently, every point has trivial stabilizer, so each [orbit](c:orbit) is in bijection with $G$.
examples: A group $G$ acts freely on itself by left multiplication.
The group $\mathbb Z$ acts freely on $\mathbb R$ by $n\cdot x=x+n$.
The group $\mathbb Z/n$ acts freely on the unit circle in $\mathbb C$ by $k\cdot z=e^{2\pi ik/n}z$.
Non-example: $SO(2)$ acting on $\mathbb R^2$ by rotations is not free, because every rotation fixes the origin.

steps: Let $G$ act freely on a nonempty set $X$, and let $g$ act as the identity map.
Pick any point $x\in X$, so that $g\cdot x=x$.
Freeness gives $g=e$, since $g\cdot x=x$.
So only the neutral element acts trivially, and the action is effective.
links.why: It shows that every free action on a nonempty set is effective, and that freeness is the stronger condition.

steps: Take a free action of $G$ on $X$, with $e\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$.
These two laws are the axioms of a [group action](c:group-action).
The free case adds that every $g\ne e$ has no fixed point.
links.why: It shows that freeness is one extra condition on an ordinary group action.

reminder: The free [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) on a set $X$ is generated by $X$ and obeys no relations except the Lie algebra axioms.
definition: The free Lie algebra $L(X)$ on a set $X$ over a field $k$ is a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) with a map $\iota:X\to L(X)$ that has the following [universal property](c:universal-property): every map from $X$ to a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ extends uniquely to a Lie algebra homomorphism $L(X)\to\mathfrak g$. One can build it as the Lie subalgebra generated by $X$ inside the free associative algebra on $X$, with the commutator as bracket.
examples: $L(\{x\})$ is the one-dimensional abelian Lie algebra spanned by $x$.
$L(\{x,y\})$ has dimension $2$ in degree $1$, dimension $1$ in degree $2$ (spanned by $[x,y]$) and dimension $2$ in degree $3$ (spanned by $[x,[x,y]]$ and $[y,[x,y]]$).
Every Lie algebra generated by a set $X$ is a quotient of the free Lie algebra $L(X)$.
Non-example: the Heisenberg Lie algebra with $[x,y]=z$ and $z$ central is generated by $x$ and $y$ but is not free, because it satisfies the extra relation $[x,z]=0$.

steps: A [free object](c:free-object) on a set $X$ comes with a universal map from $X$ into the underlying set of the object.
Here the object is a Lie algebra and the universal map is $\iota:X\to L(X)$.
The universal property says that $L$ is left adjoint to the forgetful functor from Lie algebras to sets.
links.why: It shows that the free Lie algebra is the free object for the theory of Lie algebras.

reminder: The free topological monoid on a pointed space $X$ is the space of finite words in $X$, with the basepoint as the empty word.
definition: For a [pointed space](c:pointed-space) $(X,*)$, the free topological monoid $J(X)$ is the quotient of $\bigsqcup_{n\ge0}X^n$ by the relation that deletes the basepoint from a word, with the empty word as unit and concatenation as product. It has the [universal property](c:universal-property): every pointed continuous map from $X$ to a [topological monoid](c:topological-monoid) $M$ extends uniquely to a continuous monoid homomorphism $J(X)\to M$.
examples: For $S^0=\{*,a\}$, the words are $a^n$ for $n\ge0$, so $J(S^0)\cong\mathbb N$.
For a connected CW complex $X$, the James theorem gives $J(X)\simeq\Omega\Sigma X$, so $J(S^1)\simeq\Omega S^2$ for the [loop space](c:loop-space) of $S^2$.
Non-example: the circle group $S^1$ is a topological monoid but is not $J(X)$ for any pointed space $X$, because in $J(X)$ every element other than the unit has no inverse.

steps: Let $S$ be a set, and give $S_+=S\sqcup\{*\}$ the discrete topology with basepoint $*$.
A word in $S_+$ with all basepoint letters deleted is a word in $S$.
So $J(S_+)$ is the set of finite words in $S$ with the discrete topology, with concatenation as product.
That is the [free monoid](c:free-monoid) on $S$, so the topological construction extends the algebraic one.
links.why: It shows that the free topological monoid reduces to the free monoid when the space is discrete.

reminder: An $n$-Freiman isomorphism is a bijection between sets that preserves which sums of $n$ elements are equal.
definition: Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of additive [monoids](c:monoid). An additive $n$-Freiman isomorphism from $A$ to $B$ is a [bijection](c:bijection) $f:A\to B$ such that $a_1+\cdots+a_n=a'_1+\cdots+a'_n$ holds if and only if $f(a_1)+\cdots+f(a_n)=f(a'_1)+\cdots+f(a'_n)$, for all $a_i,a'_i\in A$.
examples: Every translation $x\mapsto x+c$ and every injective group homomorphism, restricted to $A$, is an $n$-Freiman isomorphism onto its image for all $n$.
Reduction modulo $N$ is an $n$-Freiman isomorphism from a set $A\subseteq\{0,\dots,m\}$ onto its image when $nm<N$, since sums of $n$ elements stay below $N$.
Non-example: reduction modulo $4$ on $\{0,1,2,3\}$ is a bijection onto $\mathbb Z/4$ but not a $2$-Freiman isomorphism, because $1+3\ne0+0$ in $\mathbb Z$ while $1+3\equiv0+0$ modulo $4$.

reminder: The Frobenius method looks for solutions $x^r\sum_{k\ge0}a_kx^k$ of a linear equation at a regular singular point, and the indicial equation fixes $r$.
definition: Consider a second-order [linear differential equation](c:linear-differential-equation) $x^2y''+xp(x)y'+q(x)y=0$ with $p$ and $q$ analytic near the [regular singular point](c:regular-singular-point) $x=0$. The Frobenius method substitutes $y=x^r\sum_{k\ge0}a_kx^k$ with $a_0\ne0$, a [power series](c:power-series) times $x^r$. The lowest power gives the indicial equation $r(r-1)+p(0)r+q(0)=0$, and the other coefficients give a recurrence for $a_k$.
examples:
For Bessel's equation $x^2y''+xy'+(x^2-
u^2)y=0$, the indicial equation is $r^2=
u^2$, and the root $r=
u$ gives the Bessel function $J_
u$ up to a constant.
For $2xy''+y'+y=0$, the indicial roots are $0$ and $\tfrac12$, and the two series give $\cos\sqrt{2x}$ and $\sin\sqrt{2x}$.
For the Euler equation $x^2y''+axy'+by=0$, the series stops at $a_0$, and $y=x^r$ with $r^2+(a-1)r+b=0$.
Non-example: $x^2y'+y=0$ has an irregular singular point at $0$ and the solution $e^{1/x}$, and the substitution $y=x^r\sum a_kx^k$ forces $a_0=0$.

reminder: A Fuchsian group is a discrete subgroup of $PSL(2,\mathbb R)$.
definition: A Fuchsian group is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $\Gamma$ of the [projective special linear group](c:projective-special-linear-group) $PSL(2,\mathbb R)$ that is [discrete](c:discrete-group) in the matrix topology. Equivalently, $\Gamma$ acts properly discontinuously on the [upper half plane](c:upper-half-plane) by the maps $z\mapsto(az+b)/(cz+d)$, which are the orientation-preserving [isometries](c:isometry) of the [hyperbolic plane](c:hyperbolic-plane).
examples: The [modular group](c:modular-group) $PSL(2,\mathbb Z)$ is a Fuchsian group.
The cyclic group generated by $z\mapsto2z$ is a Fuchsian group.
The fundamental group of a closed surface of genus $g\ge2$ is isomorphic to a Fuchsian group with compact quotient.
Non-example: $PSL(2,\mathbb Q)$ is a subgroup of $PSL(2,\mathbb R)$ that is dense and not discrete, so it is not Fuchsian.

steps: Let $\Gamma$ be a Fuchsian group, a subgroup of the Lie group $PSL(2,\mathbb R)$.
By definition, the subspace topology on $\Gamma$ is discrete.
So $\Gamma$ is a [discrete group](c:discrete-group).
The Fuchsian case adds that $\Gamma$ sits inside $PSL(2,\mathbb R)$, so it acts on the hyperbolic plane.
links.why: It shows that Fuchsian groups are discrete groups with a fixed embedding into the isometries of the hyperbolic plane.

reminder: A functor $F$ is fully faithful when $F:\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)\to\mathrm{Hom}(FX,FY)$ is a bijection for all objects $X$ and $Y$.
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ is fully faithful when, for all objects $X,Y$ of $\mathcal C$, the map $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,Y)\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal D}(FX,FY)$ on [hom-sets](c:hom-set) is a [bijection](c:bijection). It is [faithful](c:faithful) when these maps are injective, and [full](c:full) when they are surjective.
examples: The inclusion of a [full subcategory](c:full-subcategory), such as abelian groups in groups, is fully faithful.
The [Yoneda embedding](c:yoneda-embedding) of a category into its presheaf category is fully faithful.
Every equivalence of categories is fully faithful.
Non-example: the forgetful functor from groups to sets is faithful but not full, because not every function between groups is a homomorphism.

steps: Take a fully faithful functor $F$.
Each map $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)\to\mathrm{Hom}(FX,FY)$ is a bijection, so it is injective.
Injectivity on every hom-set is the definition of a [faithful functor](c:faithful).
The fully faithful case adds surjectivity on every hom-set.
links.why: It shows that fully faithful means faithful plus full.

steps: Take a fully faithful functor $F$.
Each map $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)\to\mathrm{Hom}(FX,FY)$ is a bijection, so it is surjective.
Surjectivity on every hom-set is the definition of a [full functor](c:full).
The fully faithful case adds injectivity on every hom-set.
links.why: It shows the second half of the equation: fully faithful means full plus faithful.

steps: Let $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ be an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories), with a quasi-inverse $G$.
The natural isomorphisms $GF\cong\mathrm{id}$ and $FG\cong\mathrm{id}$ make each map $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)\to\mathrm{Hom}(FX,FY)$ a bijection.
So $F$ is fully faithful.
An equivalence adds that every object of $\mathcal D$ is isomorphic to some $FX$.
links.why: It shows that an equivalence is a fully faithful functor that also reaches every object up to isomorphism.

reminder: The function field $k(X)$ of an irreducible variety $X$ is the field of rational functions on $X$.
definition: For an irreducible [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) $X$ over a field $k$, the function field $k(X)$ is the [field of fractions](c:field-of-fractions) of the coordinate ring of any nonempty open affine subset of $X$, and it does not depend on that subset. Its elements are [rational functions](c:rational-function-on-an-affine-variety) $f/g$ with $g$ nonzero on a dense open set, and it is the local ring of $X$ at the [generic point](c:generic-point).
examples: $k(\mathbb A^n)=k(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, the field of rational functions in $n$ variables, and $k(\mathbb P^1)=k(t)$.
For the curve $X:y^2=x^3-x$ with $\mathrm{char}\,k\ne2$, $k(X)=k(x)[y]/(y^2-x^3+x)$ is a field extension of degree $2$ of $k(x)$.
The transcendence degree of $k(X)$ over $k$ is $\dim X$, so it is $2$ for the plane.
Non-example: the union $\{xy=0\}$ in the plane is reducible, and $k[x,y]/(xy)$ has zero divisors, so this variety has no function field.

reminder: The fundamental groupoid of a space has the points as objects and the homotopy classes of paths as morphisms.
definition: The fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(X)$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is the [groupoid](c:groupoid) whose objects are the points of $X$ and whose morphisms $x\to y$ are the [homotopy classes](c:homotopy-class) of [paths](c:is-path) from $x$ to $y$ that fix the endpoints. Composition is concatenation of paths, and the inverse of a class is the reversed path.
examples: For a contractible space $X$, there is exactly one morphism between any two points, so $\Pi_1(X)$ is equivalent to a point.
For the circle $S^1$, the morphisms from $x$ to $x$ form $\mathbb Z$, given by the winding number of loops.
For a discrete space $X$, $\Pi_1(X)$ has only identity morphisms.
Non-example: the set of all paths in $X$ with concatenation, before taking homotopy classes, is not a groupoid, because concatenation is not associative and paths have no strict inverses.

steps: Fix a point $x$ of $X$.
The morphisms $x\to x$ of $\Pi_1(X)$ are the homotopy classes of loops at $x$.
Composition is concatenation of loops, so these morphisms form the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) $\pi_1(X,x)$.
So the fundamental group is the automorphism group of the object $x$ in the fundamental groupoid.
links.why: It shows that the fundamental groupoid keeps all base points at once, and each fundamental group is one piece of it.

reminder: A fusion ring is a ring with a finite basis, containing $1$, whose products have non-negative integer coefficients, and a duality.
definition: A fusion ring is a [ring](c:ring) $R$ that is a [free module](c:free-module) over $\mathbb Z$ with a finite basis $\{b_i\}_{i\in I}$ that contains the unit $b_0=1$, such that $b_ib_j=\sum_kN_{ij}^kb_k$ with $N_{ij}^k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. It also has a duality, an involution $i\mapsto i^*$ of $I$ with $N_{ij}^0=\delta_{j,i^*}$ and $N_{ij}^k=N_{i^*k}^j$.
examples: The group ring $\mathbb Z[G]$ of a finite group $G$ is a fusion ring with the group elements as basis and $g^*=g^{-1}$.
The Fibonacci ring $\mathbb Z[\tau]/(\tau^2=\tau+1)$ is a fusion ring with basis $1,\tau$ and $\tau^*=\tau$.
The [Grothendieck ring](c:grothendieck-ring) of a [fusion category](c:fusion-category), such as the representations of a finite group, is a fusion ring with the simple objects as basis.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z[\tau]/(\tau^2=1-\tau)$ with basis $1,\tau$ has the structure constant $-1$ in $\tau\cdot\tau=1-\tau$, so it is not a fusion ring for this basis.

steps: A [ℤ₊-ring](c:z-ring) is a ring with a basis whose structure constants are non-negative integers and that contains $1$.
A fusion ring has such a basis, so it is a ℤ₊-ring.
The fusion case adds that the basis is finite and that a duality $i\mapsto i^*$ exists.
links.why: It shows that a fusion ring is a ℤ₊-ring with a finite basis and duals.

reminder: A $G_\delta$ subset of a space is a countable intersection of open sets.
definition: A subset $A$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a $G_\delta$ subset when $A=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}U_n$ for countably many [open sets](c:open-set) $U_n\subseteq X$. Every open set is $G_\delta$, and the complements of $G_\delta$ sets are the $F_\sigma$ sets, the countable unions of closed sets.
examples: Every open subset of $X$ is a $G_\delta$ subset.
The set of irrational numbers $\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q=\bigcap_{q\in\mathbb Q}(\mathbb R\setminus\{q\})$ is $G_\delta$ in $\mathbb R$.
In a [metric space](c:metric-space), every closed set $F$ is $G_\delta$, because $F=\bigcap_n\{x:d(x,F)<1/n\}$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Q$ is not a $G_\delta$ subset of $\mathbb R$, by the Baire category theorem.

steps: Let $U$ be an [open set](c:open-set) of $X$.
Choose every $U_n$ equal to $U$.
Then $U=\bigcap_nU_n$ is a countable intersection of open sets, so $U$ is a $G_\delta$ subset.
The $G_\delta$ case allows countably many different open sets in the intersection.
links.why: It shows that $G_\delta$ sets include all open sets and add countable intersections.

steps: A $G_\delta$ set is a countable intersection of open sets.
Open sets are [Borel sets](c:borel-set), and Borel sets are closed under countable intersections.
So every $G_\delta$ set is a Borel set.
links.why: It shows that $G_\delta$ sets are measurable for every Borel measure.

reminder: The gamma distribution with shape $k$ and scale $\theta$ has density $x^{k-1}e^{-x/\theta}/(\Gamma(k)\theta^k)$ on $x>0$.
definition: A [random variable](c:random-variable) has the gamma distribution with shape $k>0$ and scale $\theta>0$ when its [probability density function](c:probability-density-function) is $f(x)=x^{k-1}e^{-x/\theta}/(\Gamma(k)\theta^k)$ for $x>0$ and $0$ otherwise, where $\Gamma$ is the [gamma function](c:gamma-function). Its [expected value](c:expected-value) is $k\theta$ and its [variance](c:variance) is $k\theta^2$.
examples: For $k=1$, the gamma distribution is the exponential distribution with mean $\theta$.
For an integer $k$, the sum of $k$ independent exponential variables with mean $\theta$ has this distribution (the Erlang case).
The [chi-squared distribution](c:chi-squared-distribution) with $\nu$ degrees of freedom is the gamma distribution with $k=\nu/2$ and $\theta=2$.
Non-example: the [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution) is not a gamma distribution, because its density is positive on all of $\mathbb R$ while a gamma density vanishes for $x\le0$.

steps: Write the gamma density as $\exp((k-1)\log x-x/\theta-\log\Gamma(k)-k\log\theta)$ for $x>0$.
Put $T(x)=(\log x,x)$, $\eta=(k-1,-1/\theta)$ and $h(x)=1$ on $x>0$.
The density then has the form $h(x)\exp(\eta\cdot T(x)-A)$ of an [exponential family](c:exponential-family).
links.why: It shows that general facts about exponential families, such as sufficient statistics, apply to gamma distributions.

steps: Take a gamma distribution and set $k=\nu/2$ and $\theta=2$.
This is the density of the [chi-squared distribution](c:chi-squared-distribution) with $\nu$ degrees of freedom.
links.why: It shows that the chi-squared distribution is a gamma distribution with fixed scale $2$.

reminder: Gauge fixing adds a condition on the fields that picks at least one field from each gauge orbit and so removes the redundancy.
definition: In a gauge theory, fields related by a [gauge transformation](c:gauge-transformation) describe the same physical state, so they form an [orbit](c:orbit) of the [gauge group](c:gauge-group). A gauge fixing is a condition on the fields, such as $\partial_\mu A^\mu=0$, that at least one field in every orbit satisfies and, ideally, exactly one field does. The condition itself is not [gauge invariant](c:gauge-invariance), because it must separate fields of the same orbit.
examples: The [Lorenz gauge](c:lorenz-gauge) $\partial_\mu A^\mu=0$ for the electromagnetic potential.
The [Coulomb gauge](c:coulomb-gauge) $\nabla\cdot\mathbf A=0$.
The [temporal gauge](c:temporal-gauge) $A_0=0$.

Non-example: the condition $
abla	imes\mathbf A=0$ is gauge invariant, because $
abla	imes
abla\lambda=0$, so it does not choose one potential from an orbit.

steps: Let $A_\mu$ be an electromagnetic potential, with gauge transformations $A_\mu\mapsto A_\mu+\partial_\mu\lambda$.
Choose $\lambda$ as a solution of the wave equation $\Box\lambda=-\partial_\mu A^\mu$.
The new potential satisfies $\partial_\mu A'^\mu=\partial_\mu A^\mu+\Box\lambda=0$.
So every orbit contains a potential in [Lorenz gauge](c:lorenz-gauge), and the Lorenz condition is a gauge fixing.
links.why: It shows that Lorenz gauge is one gauge fixing, and why every potential can be brought into it.

steps: Let $\mathbf A$ be a vector potential, with gauge transformations $\mathbf A\mapsto\mathbf A+\nabla\lambda$.
Choose $\lambda$ as a solution of the Poisson equation $\nabla^2\lambda=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf A$.

The new potential satisfies $
abla\cdot\mathbf A'=
abla\cdot\mathbf A+
abla^2\lambda=0$.
So every orbit contains a potential in [Coulomb gauge](c:coulomb-gauge), and the Coulomb condition is a gauge fixing.
links.why: It shows that Coulomb gauge is a gauge fixing, and why it can always be reached.

reminder: The gauge group of a principal bundle is the group of its bundle automorphisms that cover the identity of the base.
definition: For a [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) $P\to X$ with [structure group](c:structure-group) $G$, the gauge group $\mathcal G(P)$ is the group of $G$-equivariant diffeomorphisms $P\to P$ that cover the identity of $X$. It is isomorphic to the group of [sections](c:section) of the [associated bundle](c:associated-bundle) $P\times_GG$, where $G$ acts on itself by conjugation. Physicists also call the structure group $G$ itself the gauge group.
examples: For the trivial bundle $X\times G$, the gauge group is the group of smooth maps $X\to G$ with pointwise product.
In electromagnetism, $G=U(1)$, and the gauge group of the trivial bundle is the group of smooth maps $X\to U(1)$, written $e^{i\lambda}$.
Over a point $X$, the gauge group is $G$ itself.
Non-example: the lift of a nontrivial diffeomorphism of the base $X$ to $P$ moves points of $X$, so it is not in the gauge group.

reminder: A quantity is gauge invariant when gauge transformations do not change it.
definition: Let a group of [gauge transformations](c:gauge-transformation) act on a space $\mathcal A$ of field configurations. A function $F$ on $\mathcal A$ is gauge invariant when $F(g\cdot A)=F(A)$ for all $A$ and all gauge transformations $g$, so $F$ depends only on the [orbit](c:orbit) of $A$.
examples:
The field strength $F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu$ is gauge invariant under $A_\mu\mapsto A_\mu+\partial_\mu\lambda$.
The Yang-Mills action $\int\mathrm{tr}(F\wedge{*F})$ is gauge invariant.
The trace of the holonomy around a closed loop, the [Wilson loop](c:wilson-loop), is gauge invariant.
Non-example: the potential $A_\mu$ itself, and the gauge-fixing term $(\partial_\mu A^\mu)^2$, change under a gauge transformation, so neither is gauge invariant.

steps: Let the group of gauge transformations act on functions $F$ on $\mathcal A$ by $(g\cdot F)(A)=F(g^{-1}A)$.
An [invariant](c:invariant) of this action is a function $F$ with $g\cdot F=F$ for every $g$.
That means $F(gA)=F(A)$ for every gauge transformation $g$.
So a gauge-invariant function is an invariant of the gauge group action on functions.
links.why: It shows that gauge invariance is the general notion of an invariant for one specific group action.

reminder: A gauge transformation changes the field variables by a local symmetry and leaves the physical state unchanged.
definition: For a [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) $P\to X$ with a [connection](c:connection) $A$, a gauge transformation is an element $g$ of the [gauge group](c:gauge-group), a bundle automorphism of $P$ that covers the identity of $X$. In a local trivialization it is a function $g:U\to G$ that sends $A$ to $gAg^{-1}+g\,d(g^{-1})$. Two connections related this way describe the same physical configuration.
examples: In electromagnetism, $A\mapsto A+d\lambda$ is a gauge transformation of the potential, with $g=e^{i\lambda}$ up to sign and charge conventions.
For $G=SU(2)$, a smooth map $g:X\to SU(2)$ acts on a connection by $A\mapsto gAg^{-1}+g\,d(g^{-1})$.
A constant $g$ is a global gauge transformation, and it acts as $A\mapsto gAg^{-1}$.
Non-example: a Lorentz transformation of spacetime changes the coordinates of the base and not the bundle, so it is not a gauge transformation.

steps: Take a gauge transformation $g:P\to P$.
It is a $G$-equivariant diffeomorphism with an inverse $g^{-1}$, so it is an [automorphism](c:automorphism) of the principal bundle.
The gauge case adds that $g$ covers the identity of the base $X$.
links.why: It shows that gauge transformations are the vertical automorphisms of a bundle, and so they form a group.

reminder: A Gauss sum is the sum $\sum_a\chi(a)e^{2\pi ia/N}$ of a multiplicative character $\chi$ against roots of unity.
definition: For a [Dirichlet character](c:dirichlet-character) $\chi$ modulo $N$, the Gauss sum is $G(\chi)=\sum_{a=0}^{N-1}\chi(a)e^{2\pi ia/N}$, a sum over $N$-th [roots of unity](c:roots-of-unity). For an odd prime $p$ and the [Legendre symbol](c:legendre-symbol) $\chi=(\cdot/p)$, this equals the quadratic Gauss sum $\sum_{a=0}^{p-1}e^{2\pi ia^2/p}$, which is $\sqrt p$ if $p\equiv1\pmod4$ and $i\sqrt p$ if $p\equiv3\pmod4$.
examples: For $p=3$, the quadratic Gauss sum is $1+2e^{2\pi i/3}=i\sqrt3$.
For $p=5$, the quadratic Gauss sum is $1+2e^{2\pi i/5}+2e^{8\pi i/5}=\sqrt5$.
For a nontrivial character $\chi$ modulo a prime $p$, $|G(\chi)|=\sqrt p$.
Non-example: the sum $\sum_{a=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ia/N}=0$ has no character weight $\chi(a)$, so it is a geometric sum and not a Gauss sum.
